title: DFS on SF SoMa: Real Streets Explored ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) “dive” through real street intersections in San Francisco’s SoMa. This DFS visualization shows stack-based backtracking and why DFS can find a path fast—or get lost exploring deep branches.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps — What happens when DFS explores real city intersections ⚡

In this visualization, each street intersection becomes a node and each road segment becomes an edge. DFS uses a stack (or recursion) to go as deep as possible along one branch, then backtracks when it hits a dead end.

Technical breakdown (what you’re seeing):
• Start at the chosen intersection (source node)
• Push neighbors in a specific order (neighbor ordering matters!)
• Visit the next unvisited neighbor immediately (deep dive)
• When no unvisited neighbors remain: backtrack (explicit stack or call stack)
• Track visited nodes to avoid cycles

Takeaway: DFS is great for “deep exploration” and connected traversal, but it’s not guaranteed to find the shortest route in weighted/road-like graphs—BFS is the usual shortest-path baseline.

Debate question: If you had to route quickly through SF streets, would you prefer DFS’s deep dive or BFS’s level-by-level sweep?
